pr_title: SSA: Applying same object twice should be a no-op the second time
pr_body:
Applying an object that doesn't make any modification, with an existing applier, shouldn't result in changes to the object. Right now, this happens because we update the time of the last apply, but it should be a no-op. This could be a problem for people applying lots of configurations.

I've included a test to show that.

We've also tagged smd as 3.0.0 for the release, so we have a clean tag now that I bumped it to that version.

issue_context.title: ensure server-side apply doesn't write to etcd if there are no changes
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
On server-side apply, we should make sure not to write to etcd if there are no changes.

For example, in this change https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88739, even though the applied object did not change, the timestamp for the field manager changed.

**What you expected to happen**:
We shouldn't update `.metadata.managedFields` if there is no change in any fields.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

```
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --server-side
sleep 1
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --server-side

# the second kubectl apply will update the field manager's timestamp and
# write to etcd even though the object didn't change
```

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): v1.17

/wg apply
/sig api-machinery
cc @apelisse @jennybuckley @kwiesmueller 

/assign @apelisse
comments: One of the original integration tests for this: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/81673

Thanks for filing this issue, it appears to be the fix I need for the following issue.  My controller uses server-side apply against an object that it is watching, and it gets into an infinite loop because it doesn't calculate whether the patch would be non-trivial.

Yes, that sounds like a side-effect of that bug. We might want to cherry-pick the fix to older release possibly. I'm not completely sure I understand why you would want to update the object anytime it changes though?

The controller is simply trying to control certain fields of a certain owned object, and so it issues a patch to that object whenever the reconciliation loop runs.   The alternative is to use pre-SSA style logic involving a 3-way merge, which I'd hoped to avoid (as per [Using Server-Side Apply in a controller](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#using-server-side-apply-in-a-controller)).

Thanks for your answer, I agree that you shouldn't have to use a three-way merge. Would you mind giving more details about what fields you're trying based on what changes? It's hard to reason without an example.

I don't mean to over-complicate, this is an ordinary situation involving an operator, a CRD, and a `Deployment`.   I simply wish to control the spec of the deployment.  If some other manager were to write an annotation onto that `Deployment`, I'd rather not overwrite it (as an `Update` would).
@apelisse are you able to take steps to backport this fix?   Honestly I don't know how to use SSA in a controller without it.

I'm planning on working on that, but I have a few other things on fire right now (so close to the 1.18 release). 

I still don't understand why a change to the object would require another change to the same object.

Also, I'm not sure I understand that: 
> If some other manager were to write an annotation onto that Deployment, I'd rather not overwrite it (as an Update would).

@apelisse maybe there's a misunderstanding.   Imagine that I have a controller which manages a resource of type `Foo`, and implements it using a resource of type `Deployment`.   The controller has a watch established for `Foo` and for `Deployment`.  Whenever the reconciliation loop runs, the controller patches the deployment using SSA to enforce a certain spec (based on information from `Foo`).   An infinite loop occurs because the patch request on the deployment causes the watch to fire, which causes the controller to patch the deployment, which causes the watch to fire, and so on.   The workaround is to use some conditional logic to avoid issuing a trivial patch, but the logic needed to do that negates the value of SSA.
Thanks, I think that's helpful. Let me see how I can cherry-pick this in previous versions.
I've tried to cherry-pick this in 1.17, but it's not that easy. There are many changes that we would have to pull along with this. I don't think I'm going to cherry-pick this.

review_comments: We're planning on inserting a Clock to mock with a fake clock and have more tests here. Not much time right now :-/
Do any managed fields updaters return a nil new object?
That's a good question. We just merged a [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/structured-merge-diff/pull/158) so that we return a `nil` new object when the object hasn't changed ...
This isn't really related to the bug, but ideally could `Update` use the same method as `Apply` to check for previous + new managed field equality? i.e. `managed.Fields().Equals(formerManaged)`
That sounds possible to be honest, what do you think @jennybuckley ?

I think it's mostly equivalent, since "self" can never own any fields before the update, if any values were changed by the update, then self would own them.

I think the only difference would be that, doing a `managed.Fields().Equals(formerManaged)` would mean we would also update the updater's timestamp if the updater removed something. Whereas the way we do it today that doesn't cause the timestamp to change
Why wouldn't the timestamp update if something is removed? That sounds like it should happen?
Will this logic continue to work if we add e.g. a "tombstone field" marker ("ensure this field doesn't exist even if I don't own it")?
